A bicycle gear system allows riders to adjust the resistance and speed of pedaling, making it easier to climb hills or maintain high speeds on flat terrain. It consists of two main components: the front chainrings (usually 1–3) attached to the pedals, and the rear sprockets (typically 7–12) on the rear wheel. These are connected by a chain that transfers power from the pedals to the rear wheel.

When you shift gears, the derailleur—a mechanism that moves the chain—shifts it between different chainrings and sprockets. Shifting to a larger front chainring and smaller rear sprocket increases gear ratio, making pedaling harder but allowing faster movement with each pedal stroke.
